problem.summary: YOLO architecture research has stayed CNN-centric because attention models cannot match CNN speed: quadratic complexity and inefficient memory access make attention too slow for real-time detectors, so its modeling benefits go unused.
statements: Attention-based models cannot match the speed of CNN-based models, so YOLO architecture work has stayed CNN-focused despite attention's proven modeling superiority.
Attention is slowed by quadratic computational complexity and inefficient memory access operations.
Under a similar computational budget, CNN-based architectures outperform attention-based ones by about 3x, limiting attention's adoption in speed-critical YOLO systems.
Attention-centric ViTs also suffer optimization problems (gradient blocking in ELAN-style aggregation) that make large models unstable or non-convergent.

evidence.quote: This is because attention-based models cannot match the speed of CNN-based models.

The primary reason for this situation lies in the inefficiency of the attention mechanism, which comes from two main factors: quadratic computational complexity and inefficient memory access operations of the attention mechanism

As a result, under a similar computational budget, CNN-based architectures outperform attention-based ones by a factor of ∼ 3× [38], which significantly limits the adoption of attention mechanisms in YOLO systems where high inference speed is critical.
Empirically, L- and X-scale models either fail to converge or remain unstable, even when using Adam or AdamW optimizers.

background.summary: The paper sits in the YOLO lineage (v6-v11) and the efficient-ViT literature (Swin, PVT, CSWin, linear attention, Mamba), and compares against end-to-end RT-DETR/RT-DETRv2, claiming prior efficient-attention designs still miss real-time speed.

relatedWork.name: YOLOv10
relatedWork.relation: immediate prior real-time YOLO with NMS-free training
relatedWork.quote: YOLOv10 [53] apply NMSfree training with dual assignments for efficiency gains.

relatedWork.name: YOLOv11
relatedWork.relation: the baseline YOLOv12 is built on and scaled with
relatedWork.quote: YOLOv11 [28] further reduces latency and increases accuracy by adopting the C3K2 module (a specification of GELAN [58]) and lightweight depthwise separable convolution in the detection head.

relatedWork.name: RT-DETR
relatedWork.quote: an end-to-end object detection method, namely RT-DETR [66], improved traditional end-to-end detectors [7, 33, 37, 42, 71] to meet realtime requirements by designing an efficient encoder and an uncertainty-minimal query selection mechanism.

relatedWork.name: Swin Transformer
relatedWork.relation: prior local/window attention design that YOLOv12's area attention replaces
relatedWork.quote: Swin Transformer [39] limits self-attention to local windows and adjusts the window partitioning style to connect non-overlapping windows, balancing communication needs with memory and computation demands.

relatedWork.name: FlashAttention
relatedWork.relation: memory-access fix adopted in the model design
relatedWork.quote: we employ FlashAttention to overcome inherent memory accessing problems of the attention mechanism [13, 14].

evidence.quote: Reducing computational costs from global self-attention is crucial to effectively applying vision transformers in downstream tasks.
Although Mamba-based vision models [38, 70] aim for linear complexity, they still fall short of real-time speeds [38].

solution.summary: YOLOv12 is an attention-centric YOLO built on three changes: an area attention module (A2) that partitions the feature map into l=4 areas instead of windows, a residual ELAN (R-ELAN) with a scaled residual shortcut to fix optimization, and vanilla-attention tweaks (FlashAttention, no positional encoding, MLP ratio 4 to 1.2, Conv+BN, 7x7 position perceiver).
solution.approach: Replace CNN-dominant YOLO blocks with a simplified area attention plus R-ELAN aggregation, keeping hierarchical YOLO structure and conv operators where they help, so attention runs at CNN-like speed.
components: Area attention (A2): feature map split into l segments (default 4), reshape-only partitioning
R-ELAN: block-level residual with 0.01 scaling and redesigned bottleneck-style feature aggregation
MLP ratio reduced from 4 to 1.2 (2 for N/S/M)
nn.Conv2d+BN instead of nn.Linear+LN attention implementation
No positional encoding; 7x7 separable-convolution position perceiver
Single R-ELAN block in the last backbone stage instead of stacked blocks

evidence.quote: we propose a simple yet efficient area attention module (A2), which maintains a large receptive field while reducing the computational complexity of attention in a very simple way, thus enhancing speed.
we introduce a residual shortcut from input to output throughout the block with a scaling factor (default to 0.01).
These modifications include adjusting the MLP ratio from 4 to 1.2 (or 2 for the N- / S- / M-scale models) is used to better allocate computational resources for better performance
removing positional encoding, and introduce a large separable convolution (7 × 7) (namely position perceiver) to help the area attention perceive position information.

experiments.summary: Five YOLOv12 scales are trained 600 epochs on COCO 2017 and compared with YOLOv6/8/9/10/11, Gold-YOLO and RT-DETR/RT-DETRv2 on AP, FLOPs, parameters and TensorRT FP16 T4 latency, plus ablations and speed tests on RTX 3080/A5000/A6000 and CPU.

evidence.quote: YOLOv12-N achieves 40.6% mAP with an inference latency of 1.64 ms on a T4 GPU, outperforming advanced YOLOv10-N / YOLOv11-N by 2.1%/1.2% mAP with a comparable speed.
YOLOv12-S beats RT-DETR-R18 / RT-DETRv2- R18 while running 42% faster, using only 36% of the computation and 45% of the parameters.

For N-scale models, YOLOv12-N outperforms YOLOv6-3.0-N [32], YOLOv8-N [58], YOLOv10-N [53], and YOLOv11 [28] by 3.6%, 3.3%, 2.1%, and 1.2% in mAP, respectively, while maintaining similar or even fewer computations and parameters, and achieving the fast latency speed of 1.64 ms/image.

limitations.summary: The main admitted limitation is dependency on FlashAttention, which restricts supported GPUs; training also needs about 600 epochs and large models need a tuned residual scaling factor to converge.
items: Requires FlashAttention, which only supports Turing/Ampere/Ada Lovelace/Hopper GPUs (T4, RTX 20/30/40, A5000/6000, A30/40, A100, H100, etc.).
Needs a longer training schedule (about 600 epochs) than the roughly 500 epochs some YOLO detectors need for peak performance.
Large models (L/X) depend on a residual scaling factor of 0.01 to converge at all.
Results are reported only on MS COCO with the standard YOLO recipe and no additional tricks.

evidence.quote: YOLOv12 requires FlashAttention [13, 14], which currently supports Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, or Hopper GPUs (e.g., T4, Quadro RTX series, RTX20 series, RTX30 series, RTX40 series, RTX A5000/6000, A30/40, A100, H100, etc.).
YOLOv12 requires a more extended training period (about 600 epochs) to achieve peak performance
YOLOv12-X requires a minimal scaling factor (0.01) to ensure convergence.

futureDirections.direction: Continue integrating attention into YOLO for a more efficient and powerful YOLO system.
futureDirections.quote: advances the integration of attention mechanisms for real-time object detection, paving the way for a more efficient and powerful YOLO system.

backbones: hierarchical YOLO backbone (first two stages inherited from YOLOv11)

equations.expr: 2 n^2 h d -> 2 n h d^2

applications.detail: Positioned as a low-latency real-time detector whose speed characteristics make it practically deployable.
applications.quote: Real-time object detection has consistently attracted significant attention due to its low-latency characteristics, which provide substantial practicality [4, 17, 24, 28].

deploymentClaims: YOLOv12-N runs at 1.64 ms inference latency (40.6 mAP) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU.
Latency measured with TensorRT FP16 on T4; also benchmarked on RTX 3080, RTX A5000, RTX A6000 and an Intel Core i7-10700K CPU.
YOLOv12-S uses 45% of RT-DETR-R18 parameters and 36% of its computation while running 42% faster.
Trained on 8x NVIDIA A6000 GPUs; official code released at github.com/sunsmarterjie/yolov12.

evidence.quote: the latencies of all models are tested on a T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16.
All models are trained on 8× NVIDIA A6000 GPUs.
